# heartwood-ledger

> Running a Nostr signer means trusting a daemon or an ESP32 with your key.
> heartwood-ledger moves that trust boundary onto a Ledger Nano S+: NIP-44
> decrypt, NIP-46 dispatch and kind:24133 envelope signing all happen inside
> the secure element, gated by on-device approval.
>
> Prototype: emulator-proven (Speculos), not yet run on a physical device;
> sideload only. Nano S+ is the only target built and tested; Nano X is listed
> in the manifest but untested, and Stax and Flex are not targeted.

It is for people already running the [Heartwood](https://github.com/forgesworn/heartwood)
Nostr signer stack who want the ESP32/ESP8266 hardware replaced with a Ledger
they may already own. It shares its NIP-44, NIP-46, derivation and identity
logic with the ESP32 firmware through the `heartwood-common` crate, compiled
unmodified for the Ledger target, so restoring a Heartwood seed phrase through
Ledger's own onboarding produces the identical npub and
[nsec-tree](https://github.com/forgesworn/nsec-tree) personas.

## Getting Started

Build and prove the app with Docker (no local Ledger toolchain install):

```sh
git clone https://github.com/forgesworn/heartwood-ledger
git clone https://github.com/forgesworn/heartwood-esp32   # sibling checkout, path dependency
cd heartwood-ledger
./scripts/e2e.sh
```

`scripts/e2e.sh` builds the app for Nano S+, boots it in Speculos seeded with
the canonical all-zero test phrase, and runs the host interop driver against
it. Sideloading onto a physical device is not yet covered; see README.md.

## Key Concepts

- **Same identity as the ESP firmware.** The master key is the BIP-32 node at
  `m/44'/1237'/727'/0'/0'`, the path the ESP firmware, provision CLI and
  sapwood all derive from.
- **TOFU signing policy.** Non-signing methods (`get_public_key`, NIP-44/04
  encrypt/decrypt) never prompt. The first `sign_event` from an unknown client
  blocks on an on-device Approve/Reject screen; approval stores the client and
  grants unattended signing thereafter.
- **Keys never leave the device.** Derivation goes through
  `os_perso_derive_node_bip32`; the OS restricts the app to the `44'/1237'`
  subtree.

## API Surface

The app exposes an APDU protocol (CLA `0xE0`), documented in `src/main.rs` and
in the README.md "APDU protocol" section (P1/P2 flags, status words, framing):

- `GET_VERSION` (`0x03`): returns `[major, minor, patch]`.
- `GET_APP_NAME` (`0x04`): returns `b"Heartwood"`.
- `GET_PUBKEY` (`0x05`): returns the 32-byte x-only master pubkey.
- `PROCESS` (`0x10`, chunked): P1 is the chunk index from 0, P2 is `0x80` for
  more chunks and `0x00` for the last; the host driver sends 250-byte chunks
  (APDU limit 255) and the app enforces an 8 KiB total. It accumulates an `ENCRYPTED_REQUEST` body; on the last chunk it
  decrypts, dispatches the NIP-46 request, signs the response envelope and
  replies with the result length as a big-endian `u16`.
- `GET_RESULT` (`0x11`, chunked): P1 is the chunk index from 0; each reply is
  the next slice of up to 250 bytes of the `SIGN_ENVELOPE_RESPONSE` JSON. Read
  until you hold the length from `PROCESS`; a chunk index past the end returns
  `0xB013`.

An on-device Reject is not a status word: `PROCESS` returns `0x9000` and the
signed envelope carries the NIP-46 error `-32000` `denied at device`.

`heartwood-bridge` (branch `ledger-transport`) speaks this protocol directly
over TCP or USB HID; see README.md "Using it with the bridge".
